concept.name: Tick rule
concept.definition: A trade-classification heuristic that signs a trade as buyer-initiated if its price is above the previous trade price (uptick) and seller-initiated if below (downtick), carrying the sign of the last nonzero price change through zero ticks. It is one of the component rules evaluated in Lee and Ready (1991).
concept.intuition: Rising prints suggest buyers are pushing the price up; falling prints suggest sellers are pushing it down.
concept.mechanics: Compare each trade price to the previous one: an uptick signs the trade positive, a downtick negative, and an unchanged price inherits the sign of the most recent nonzero change. It requires only the trade price series, not quote data.
concept.formula: s_t = sign(P_t - P_{t-1}); if P_t = P_{t-1}, s_t = s_{last nonzero change}.
concept.failure_modes: It misclassifies trades that move within the quote range (bid-ask bounce reversals) and cannot see where a trade sits relative to the spread; Lee and Ready find quote-based classification generally more accurate.
concept.misconceptions: An uptick does not prove a market buy occurred - a trade can tick up while executing inside a rising quote range, so tick signs are noisy proxies for aggressor direction.
concept.example: Prints of 50.00, 50.01, 50.01, and 49.99 are signed +1, +1 (zero tick inherits), and -1.

citations.source: Lee and Ready, 'Inferring Trade Direction from Intraday Data', Journal of Finance 46(2):733-746 (course-hosted copy)
